subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the minister who has just spoken that I am quite optimistic and I hope that his fine words will be followed by good results.
It is difficult and probably useless to deal with a special point in the national budget and to appreciate it in relation to the whole national economy. I find it more convenient to consider the budget as a whole with its general policies and trends, to determine whether it will give the results expected by the people, because finally it is for the entire population that the ministers and members of this House pass and administer pieces of legislation and bring down budgets.
Now, when everybody have been complaining about inflation, unemployment poverty, low salaries or excessive income taxes for over 20 years, can it be said that this budget is effecting a better distribution of revenues, taxes and profits capitalized by the Canadian citizens?
That is the crux of the matter. Mr. Speaker, I have every reason to believe that we must not fight inflation, that we must not fight unemployment, that we must not do away with poverty. All those aims are negative, jarring, depressing. Unity of action demands that our efforts be oriented toward achieving a balanced national economy through balance between individuals, families and all Canadian citizens including the government of Canada. That is positive; single-mindedness of purpose, that is an exalting objective.
In my humble opinion, the measures announced in the budget are not the best means of facing up to the present economic situation. They will not do enough to ensure our economic recovery.
In this regard, I read, on June 25 last, in the newspaper Le Droit, the following comments made by Mr. Don Montgomery, secretary-treasurer of the Canadian Labour Congress. I quote:
The budget gives Canadians no reason to believe the government is making an effort to deal with inflation of higher unemployment.
And I agree with him. If we consider that we are living now in the most unsettled economic climate of the past 30 years, we readily recognize that the legislation proposed by the government is far from being adequate.
Mr. Speaker, we are certainly aware that inflation has been over the past few years the most pressing economic problem industrialized nations of the world have had to face. We are also aware that this phenomenon has been the subject of interminable and endless discussions and debates. To end up with what? Nothing but detrimental effects on the Canadian economy.

As a matter of fact, in the June 20, 1975 issue of the daily La Presse, Senator Maurice Lamontagne, a seasoned economist and former federal minister, was quoted as saying:
The economic forecasts of the federal government over the past 20 years proved constantly wrong; what is more, this government never had any true policy.
Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt that the government has been taking all sorts of steps for many years to reduce the level of inflation. Unfortunately, it has now come to realize somewhat readily that its efforts and restrictive measures will not spare us this disaster.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, we must admit that there are in the June 23 budget a number of very valid measures, including those concerning the monitoring of public expenses. For once indeed the government will try to restrict the growth of its expenditures. I seize the opportunity to congratulate the minister for his initiative and his expressed intention of cutting federal government spending by $1 billion during the present fiscal year.
With regard to housing, I was very pleased to hear the minister had allocated some $200 million more to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, as well as larger grants for housing units financed by the private sector. But unfortunately, I realize it is far from being sufficient. Besides, Chamber of Commerce Chairman Sam Hughes confirmed it when he said that the supplementary $200 million for housing are not enough. Moreover, we find no aid whatever is provided in the budget for the great number of those who buy existing houses.
Mr. Speaker, if every Canadian is to be able to afford the minimum requirement in housing-a decent home under normal terms, I sincerely believe the Minister of Finance should have introduced measures with a view to reducing the very high interest rates and making capital more readily available to all citizens, since dwellings and houses are an essential part of human life. Indeed they are absolutely necessary to all Canadians, because we constantly have to fight the hazards and severity of winter. All Canadians must have a home of their own where they can live conveniently. There is no use hiding the fact: the present budgetary measures, which contain no particular incentive for bettering the Canadian economy, have their greatest effect on low-income citizens.
I think immediately of the new tax on petroleum products and its equivalents. This measure will undoubtedly contribute much to worsen inflation and it will affect mostly the small wage-earners who already do not have sufficient purchasing power. I believe that this measure is the most unfavourable one of the budget since it is the strictest and it affects all Canadians. In this regard, on June 25 last, in the newspaper Le Droit, we could read the following:
The gasoline price increase will have a psychological effect on people. The public will always remember that the Turner budget reduced the purchasing power. Higher gasoline prices will have the most serious effects on the worker who must often use his car to go to work.
Mr. Speaker, this measure places a heavy burden on all car drivers, especially those with an average income. The government is unjustly squeezing taxpayers who cannot afford this increase. The government could easily have obtained the $500 million it will take from these poor
July 4, 1975

people by taxing the large multinational companies to effect a fairer redistribution of our country's wealth.
Under the circumstances, the government is forcing car drivers to use public transportation. I find this very unfair since 85 per cent of Canadians use their car either to go to work or for business trips. Moreover, I believe that this increase could also result in considerable losses for vacation centres and business in general.
What is most regrettable is that the minister has provided no allocation to help people from 60 to 65 who are unemployed or unable to find work. Yet, those are the people who are but hardest by inflation. In agriculture, there is no measure aiming at correcting the present mess.
I sincerely think that one of the good means of slowing down inflation, and by the same occasion of alleviating the international food crisis, would have been to give increased help to Canadian farmers.
Since most of the time they are harassed by controls of all kinds and had to have a lot of courage to hold on to a farm, even though it offers a lot of possibilities, I consider the government must give farmers security and introduce immediate steps to correct the situation, either by being more flexible under the farm improvement loan program, or by government investment into research, or still by better financial terms that could allow under cultivated land to be improved. In fact, no concrete effort was made to help the farming community through financial incentives. That is basically the problem. It has a solution and the solution can come only from us in the Parliament of Canada. Why then continue again this year to introduce a budget that reduces the purchasing power of the population and increases the annual deficit of the government itself?
The poor will become poorer and further deny themselves. The government will go deeper into debt so large corporations and the directors and main shareholders will become even richer and accumulate more capital.
That direction which dates back many years must be changed. The decision rests with us. We are responsible for distributive justice, the natural resources that belong to everyone and the work of the adult and qualified population which deserves decent incomes.
If we do not take our responsibilities for a fairer distribution of incomes, who is going to take them for us? That is the only question we must answer here if we really want to curb inflation, unemployment and poverty and replace them with national economic balance between incomes, expenditures and profits between individuals and families.
There is no point in talking about anything else. This must be settled first, and then we can improve production and capitalization. But let us first give full satisfaction to consumers.
Mr. Speaker, if the government wish to plan a well-balanced long term policy, if they really wish to slow down inflation, they should undoubtedly implement the active and efficient measures which the Social Credit Party of Canada has been advocating for a number of years. When I talk about active measures, I am referring to the establishment of the guaranteed income system which would no doubt provide every Canadian citizen with a
The Budget-Mr. C. Smith
form of security. I also suggest that anyone who wishes to retire at 60 should be allowed to do so on an optional basis.
This would have the effect of providing a number of young people with jobs, since the lowering of retirement age would make way for many employment opportunities.
Mr. Speaker, the government should right away and once and for all implement highly commendable measures on the basis of our proposals. I was suggesting more or less the same things in 1973 and 1974 in my speeches which were put in the record on various dates, but I seem to be misunderstood. We should remove every obstacle and honestly face our responsibilities as ministers or members of Parliament. This fairly sums up the expectations of Canadian citizens who long for social justice, a united Canada and a balanced economy which would make the people happy. The people of Canada wish peace with order and order in life.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will notice that I have written my remarks in red as I feel that this government is trying to draw the last ounce of blood from the consumer.
June 23 is a day I will long remember, and I am sure millions of Canadians will not forget it easily. The first reason I will remember June 23 is not that it was my birthday but it was the day of the disaster budget which spelled doom for people living in the northern parts of Canada where the cost of living is now completely out of control. It gave me little comfort, and certainly it gave no comfort to the people of the Churchill constituency, to hear of the ten cents per gallon excise tax. When the minister spoke of $2 per gallon gas in Great Britain he should have had some of the facts straight about Canada. He should at least have known that the price of gas in some northern parts of Canada, especially the Churchill constituency, is well over $2 per gallon at the present time. That does not include the tax that went into effect on June 24; that price was already in place in some of the northern communities. A further 10 or 15 cents per gallon excise tax will be imposed when deliveries are received next winter.
The cost of living is high in the north; in fact, it has reached the point where it is almost impossible to encourage people to come north to fill the jobs that are available. When I speak of this two bucks a gallon gas and what it is doing to the north and the people there who are trying to make ends meet, I am sure this government did not give them any thought. Many of our northern towns and cities have no public transit system and people are forced to use their cars or boats for transportation. This government appears to make its policy around that great corridor from Montreal to Windsor, and it could not care less about the rest of Canada-especially the north where courageous men and women are trying to develop a little more of this great country of ours.
This government is not working with the people of Canada, Mr. Speaker; it is working against the consumer who is out trying to earn an honest living. In the north there is no downhill; this budget has made the going so tough that it is an uphill grind all the way.

July 4, 1975
The Budget-Mr. C. Smith
Mr. Speaker, I come now to one of the most disastrous areas of this budget, and that is the additional tax on heating fuel.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In northern Canada, where consumers are forced to heat their homes for 914 or 10 months of the year, this government has accomplished one thing at least-it has wrestled the consumer to the ground.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It would appear that this government is not interested in the development of northern Canada and the people who live there. This is reflected in the additional $200 million which was made available for housing. Many of the northern communities have such critical housing shortages that people are living in tents. Will any of this $200 million reach the northern part of Canada? We will never see a cent-it will all be used up in some of the urban centres. I have spoken several times on the development of log homes in some areas of northern Manitoba and northern Canada as a means of relieving the housing shortage. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) agrees that it would be one way of meeting some of the problems, but this government has not seriously looked at the development of this type of housing for the north.
There are other aspects of the budget that I should like to comment on, but time does not permit me to do so. One thing I should mention, though, is that many of the northern mining communities have almost reached their limit of existence. Metals are being marketed for half the cost of production. How much longer can that go on? I would suggest a year and a half or two years at the outside.
I was happy with some parts of the budget, however. I was happy to see that some $70 million will be added for training in industry and educational institutions. I hope that a substantial portion of these funds will be used to initiate meaningful training for our native people in the north. Many are now unemployed and are willing to go to work, but they need training. The training programs at the present time are outdated and do not meet the needs of our native and northern people.
The budget has shown that additional funds will be made available through local initiative programs. I notice this is now called Local Initiative Programs Operations and I wonder if it will be another abbreviated-title program called LIPO. I welcome this proposal, provided the funds are directed to projects that will be of long-term benefit to the communities in which they are established. Last year one community asked if they could use some of their approved LIP grant to complete a housing program that had been started during the summer and was not completed because of lack of funds. Permission was refused because the program did not meet the criteria for the LIP grant. I have never heard of a more ridiculous situation than people who do not have a roof over their heads being denied permission to spend money that has been approved for the community to put roofs on houses. I would suggest the community should have more authority and control over these funds.

Transportation in the north has been struck another blow due to the reduction of capital expenditures. This will mean that work will stop on northern transportation facilities, including airstrips. Cutbacks have already started. Another blow has been struck, and I say it is a blow below the belt. As Canada was celebrating Canada Day on July 1, many people in the Churchill riding had nothing to celebrate because on that day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) cancelled all schedule II and III licences of air carriers into at least 15 of the northern airstrips in the vast riding of Churchill.
To add insult to injury, Madam Speaker, the budget imposed an additional 3 per cent tax on air transportation in Canada and to the United States. This iss being imposed upon people who have no other means of transportation from their communities. When he came up with this little gem, the minister never gave a thought to those people. This is a complete disaster. It is a double blow aimed at people who live in northern Canada, especially northern Manitoba.
I could think of many things the government could do to show restraint. Let me mention one of them. It could postpone the metric conversion program for a couple of years. This would not affect too many people, and would save millions of dollars. Madam Speaker, I hope the minister will consider my remarks.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is with some sadness that I rise to participate in the debate on the budget. I am sad because the Government of Canada has refused to show able, decisive leadership, and because under the present Liberal government it appears that the leadership we do have is attempting to destroy the country, or at least cripple it by steering the ship of state on to the rocks.
I am particularly distressed because, over-all, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduced, on June 23, some very retrogressive tax measures which will cost the average working person some $300 per year out of his or her "after tax" income, if you consider the increase in automotive fuel costs, heating fuel costs, increased unemployment insurance premiums and so on. Surely by taking that much out of a taxpayer's after tax income the government is not only fuelling but encouraging inflation, by inviting another round of increased wage demands. The government has been creating money and spending it foolishly over the last few years. Now, in the midst of a recession, the chickens have come home to roost.
I find, Madam Speaker, that I must condemn the government for putting the burden of its past errors and ineptitude on the shoulders of the working man and the consuming public. To use a bad phrase for a bad budget, the Minister of Finance's budget must be termed "a gas".
The Minister of Finance's portfolio has never been popular, the reason being usually that the Minister of Finance must show guts and leadership. Frequently he must introduce unpopular measures and hold in check his free-spending cabinet colleagues in order to keep the economy ticking smoothly. So far the Minister of Finance has retained a large measure of popularity. He wants to bol-
July 4, 1975

ster his position as heir apparent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). That he wants to succeed the Prime Minister in office has never been doubted. To this end, remaining popular is all-important to the minister. I have come to the conclusion in the last few months, regretfully, that our Minister of Finance has put his own popularity, his own ambitions, ahead of the well being of Canada.
In the three and a half years since the Minister of Finance assumed his office we have had five budgets, an unheard of number in such a small time span. In the 40 months since the Minister of Finance took office inflation has risen from an annual rate of 4.2 per cent to a rate of about 12 per cent; government spending increased by 99.5 per cent; the money supply increased by 45.7 per cent; government revenues from personal income tax increased by over 90 per cent; and unemployment increased, with about 200,000 extra people becoming unemployed. In those 40 months lack of leadership and mismanagement of our economy caused the Consumer Price Index to increase by 32.6 per cent. This inflation triggered excessive wage and salary demands and led, in turn, to labour unrest. There is so much labour unrest in Canada that we are in the unenviable position of having lost more working days through strikes than any western industrialized nation, except Italy.
Really, I don't give a hoot for the minister, personally, or for the government. But it is sad to see that they have made the whole country pay heavily for their errors and omissions.
When the minister took office some 40 months ago, it was said that Canada's living standard was the second highest in the world. Now we are considered to have the sixth highest standard of living. Now the chickens have come home to roost.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which are the other five countries?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This budget is excessively cruel to the average working Canadian, but it only tinkers with inflation and unemployment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which are the other five countries?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member opposite be so kind as to shut his mouth until I have finished? He may ask his question then.
In the last 40 months the Minister of Finance brought down four budgets, besides the one we are considering. Those budgets all dealt with themes. The theme of the 1972 budget was that of controlling prices. What happened? The theme of the 1973 budget was that of reducing inflation. What happened? The theme of the May, 1974, budget was that of increasing the supply of goods and services to combat inflation. What happened? The theme of the November, 1974, budget was that of increasing productivity, to keep inflation down and combat rising unemployment. Not one of those budgets fulfilled its expressed intentions. Not one accomplished what it said it would accomplish. They did not live up to their self-proclaimed, glowing expectations.
What do we have in the budget of June 23, 1975? Its theme must be that of government self-restraint. Using a certain amount of double talk, a bit of the old sleight of
The Budget-Mr. Dick
hand and a fair bit of deceit, the Minister of Finance said he would try to cut government expenditures by $1 billion. If the average Canadian arranged his financial affairs in the way the minister said on Monday, June 23, the government is to arrange this country's financial affairs, that little old average Canadian would be charged with fraud or false pretences. Actually, while the minister spoke I could sense that he knew that what he was saying just did not add up to the full truth.
For the first time in modern Canadian history a minister of finance when bringing down a budget failed to give us any projections. He failed to predict the growth, or retraction, of the Canadian economy, the rate of inflation next year, how many housing starts there would be, or what the unemployment rate would be. I suspect he failed to predict these things because such predictions would tend to show what a mess this Liberal government has got us into.
The only thing he predicted-he had to, because in essence the budget must show how many dollars are coming in and how many are going out-was the biggest deficit in our history, some $5.3 billion.
Let me talk about the theme of this budget, restraint in government spending. Let us consider that proposed $1 billion cut. The figures set out on page 15 of the budget booklet add up to $880 million, not $1 billion, and those figures are so fuzzy as to be unreal. What is meant by the statement that $100 million is to be cut from the expenditures of the Departments of Transport, Defence, Public Works, Environment and others? Which are the others? How much is to be cut from each department, and where? How can you cut Department of Transport spending and keep your election commitments to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on transportation? It's a bit of a mess, isn't it? And which are "the others" mentioned in that paragraph which speaks about cutting $250 million? And isn't it nice to cut $350 million from the spending of some four Crown corporations which have not even been incorporated by law, proclaimed, or otherwise set up, and cannot even receive the funds? I see a nice little bit of deception there. The government has not cut a thing out of the estimates; at best it has postponed expenditures.
Madam Speaker, I say this to the minister through you, of course: if you really wanted to cut spending, why not hack away at that $1 billion paid annually for outside consultant fees-or would that mess up the Liberal party's pork barrel? We should remember that our public service is one of the best in the world; so why do the Liberals forget it? Why not prune government printing expenses? I do not need every government document in five living full colours. And why not cut out Beryl Plumptre, Information Canada, and helicopter flights by the Prime Minister? Those things add up and would be a lot more honest. It can hardly be called government restraint when last November the minister said federal expenditures would go up 15.7 per cent, and now he says that in fact we are going to restrain our federal expenditures to an increase of 16.8 per cent. That is an increase, John-boy, not restraint.
In fact, on reading pages 13, 14 and 15 in the minister's nicely bound budget speech, I had to pinch myself in order

July 4, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Dick
to make sure that I was not in dreamland. The words are impressive, they cling together well. However, on those pages the government did not take a steadfast intransigent stand to even cut that illusory $1 billion.
It states, and I quote:
Our target of cuts this fiscal year is $1 billion.
The word is "target" not "will", and the government has never hit one of its "targets" yet. This Minister of Finance has said he is aiming at a target. He does not commit himself and the government to cutting $1 billion. Therefore, we see that there is a bit of sleight-of-hand at work in the reference to that so-called $1 billion.
Let me say a few words about fuel costs and taxes thereon. The total cost of increasing the well-head cost per barrel and the ten cents excise tax per gallon will probably work out to somewhere between 15 and 18 cents per gallon of gas, probably closer to the 18 cents than the 15 cents. This increase, along with the increase in natural gas for heating fuel, will probably cause the Consumer Price Index, or cost of living, to rise almost 2 per cent in the next 12 months. That is only one commodity. Is that what you call curbing inflation? The ten cents a gallon excise tax will generate, the minister says, some $350 million, but he does not say how much it will cost to administer. Administration of the rebates under the program will eat up a healthy portion. While the government keeps the money, individuals, companies and small independent businessmen will have to borrow money at 11 to 13 per cent interest until they get their rebates back-another cost factor to add to inflation.
It would be unparliamentary for me to say the Minister of Finance lied or deliberately misled the House in saying that these measures would help conserve gasoline consumption, so I won't say that. However, I can say that the minister by sleight-of-hand did deceive the House in making us believe that energy conservation was a high priority in his mind, when on page 32 of the minister's nicely bound budget speech, the third paragraph commences:
The increased cost of gasoline resulting from these measures shall encourage motorists to make their driving habits more efficient in terms of saving gasoline.
Later, after a lot of mumble jumble about conservation of fuels, he adds:
Both improved driving practices-can make significant contributions to needed fuel conservation.
At the next question period on June 25 he admitted that he had taken these steps without making any estimation of any fuel conservation which would result, and he admitted as reported at page 7043 of Hansard:
The primary purpose of the tax is to pay for a single oil price in Canada.
In other words, the tax is to raise revenue, not a cent of which will go to the producing provinces, the oil companies, or to help find new sources of oil. I should point out that the Minister of Finance had the effrontery to add:
The increased cost of gasoline will also encourage use of public transportation.
A few pages earlier, he said he is going to cut part of this $1 billion from the Department of Transport, and he completely ignored in this budget speech the Liberal party's

multi-million dollar pledge in the last election of assistance for mass transit.
Every worker in medium sized cities, towns, villages, and in the countryside and elsewhere who has to motor to work will be paying this extra 15 or so cents a gallon, not only while on his way to or from work but when generally driving around. I hope they remember who put this extra cost on their budget. Perhaps we should all have a bumper sticker on our car to the effect "Buy a Liberal gallon of gas, only 15 cents more".
I would point out that I received a resolution from the Municipality of the Township of North Elmsley which reads as follows:
Whereas a budget was introduced by the finance minister for Canada on June 24, 1975;
And whereas included in the said budget was provision for an immediate additional excise tax of ten cents upon each gallon of auto gasoline sold in Canada, supposedly designed to encourage the use by Canadians of mass transit systems;
And whereas residents of rural municipalities in Canada are unable to avail themselves of mass transit systems, and as a result, the budget is extremely discriminatory against rural residents,
Be it resolved that the council of the township of North Elmsley write immediately to the finance minister for Canada to register violent objection to the said budget.
These added fuel costs are directly inflationary and will cost jobs, and cause hardship to the average working Canadian. These costs discriminate against those in areas other than the large metropolitan centres.
When debate arises on amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act I will have more to say, but briefly may I protest the government's decision to let itself off the hook by changing the 4 per cent benchmark to one of an eight year floating average which will mitigate the government's responsibility and lessen its financial stake in trying to improve our sad unemployment figures. It has been estimated that the government's decision to change this act in the way it has proposed will cost every working man an increase in premiums from a low of $48 per year to an average high of $89 per year per worker. This is a direct tax on the working man and on the company or small business with whom he is employed. It is unwarranted and is a dereliction of the government's responsibility.
I do not disagree with the government's decision to force an extended penalty on those who quit work or refuse employment, but if the government wants to clean up the mess in unemployment insurance which it itself created, it should start by having a full public inquiry so that unions, employers, people unemployed, and generally the public at large can have some input. I suggest that as part of this the government might reconsider requiring people to work for 12 or 16 weeks before they can make a claim rather than the present unsatisfactory eight week period. At the same time, it could improve the legislation by straightening out the first and second phases of an initial claim. This re-instated second phase so many weeks after an initial claim leads to too many problems and is in the main discriminatory.
I am most concerned about the inadequate stimulus to the housing sector in this budget. The amount the government has re-directed toward housing is not enough considering the plight of thousands of inadequately housed Canadians and the state of this industry. Instead of drop-
July 4, 1975

ping the 5 per cent tax on insulation materials, which will probably amount to approximately a $25 saving per house, the minister should have taken off all federal taxes on building materials. His budget will probably result in the bidding up of the housing which is presently available and, because the government is going to have to borrow $5.3 billion to cover its deficit, the budget will probably force up mortgage rates on the limited capital markets available in this country.
Most people want lower interest rates, and my party's suggestion in the last election of allowing people to deduct the interest paid on a mortgage over 8 per cent, to a maximum of $1,000, from taxable income would be a better way to stimulate the housing industry than any of the suggestions the minister has made in his budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have pointed out a few of the problems that this country faces because of this budget, the deception in which the budget was conceived, and the failure of the Minister of Finance in his previous budgets. I have talked briefly about the so-called government restraints, the taxes on gasoline and other fuels, and the unfair tax on the working man, companies, and small businessmen through the changing of the Unemployment Insurance Act as proposed. I have dealt briefly with housing, and would have liked to have talked about the government's copping out of medicare and forcing the burden for payment on to the provinces. Hopefully another occasion will give me an opportunity to talk about the government's intent toward our hospitalization and medicare plan.
If there are failures, the failures are of the very things about which the Minister of Finance has boasted in his budget he will do. The failures are that the government has not, in fact, cut any government spending; the government has not set an example, and has not shown any real restraint. Madam Speaker, the government says it was seeking a consensus. I hope the government remembers that it cannot find consensus when it spends millions of dollars of taxpayers' money trying to knock the very consensus it is seeking. May I say, finally, that I am very regretful that the government has used so much ad hocery in setting up so many temporary, so-called job creation programs. The money, I believe, could have been used in a more beneficial and lasting way in so many other areas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I see little point in dealing with the remarks made by the previous speaker. They have been answered many times before by members on this side, as well as answered very competently by others who have spoken in this budget debate.
My first words on the budget are to repeat in this House the congratulations which I expressed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on Monday evening, June 23. I voiced my approval of his approach to the serious problems facing us and my support for the measures which are being introduced.
The Budget-Mr. Herbert
Much publicity has been given to the increased prices for gasoline, natural gas, and heating oil. When the price equalization policy was introduced, our imports and exports of oil were in approximate balance. Now, as imports have increased while exports have decreased, the oil export tax deficit has gone to some $400 to $600 million. Without the $1.50 increase to $8 a barrel, the deficit would have approached $1 billion per annum. Clearly this was an unacceptable situation. Also it was apparent that prebudget gas and oil prices were not discouraging consumption.
I have posed the question to my constituents, and I do so to every consumer in the province of Quebec: is there any justification for a government subsidy, paid by every taxpayer, that encourages rather than discourages the use of imported fuel, fuel for which we pay dearly with our Canadian dollars? Is it not more logical to seek means by which we can keep our own dollars in our own province, in our own country? Changing our habits to decrease our consumption of foreign fuels would also help our balance of payments, which has deteriorated due to the increased cost of imports and the decrease in our exports.
Let me suggest how almost everyone in Quebec can assist. Is it logical that we should continue to heat our homes with costly imported fuel when we have an ample supply of a renewable resource in our own province? Most of my constituents were subsidized last winter in home heating oil to the extent of from $100 to $150. For my own home I estimate the subsidy to have been in the order of $250. Would it not make more sense to encourage conversion to electric heating? What is the logic in having my fellow taxpayers contribute $250 to subsidize my home heating so that I can send my dollars to Venezuela and the Arab countries?
I am sure my own constituents will appreciate my next point. A high voltage electrical line is to cross the beautiful countries of Vaudreuil and Soulanges to export surplus electricity to the United States. At the new oil price of $8 a barrel, it is not more expensive to heat by electricity than by imported oil-and it should not be forgotten that at the $8 price the subsidy is still approximately 12 cents per gallon.
I sincerely hope that the removal of the federal tax on insulation materials will encourage Quebeckers to help their province and their country by converting to electric heating. There has been opposition expressed to the imposition of the 10 cents a gallon excise tax on gasoline for the private automobile. Let me reiterate here that this tax will not affect farmers, business, construction projects, or commercial transportation. Is it not entirely logical that the consumers of gasoline pay according to the amount they use? Do not the majority of car drivers have a choice in reducing their consumption? Even with the additional 10 cents a gallon excise tax, the price is still below the imported cost.
I see no logic whatsoever in subsidizing the private car driver when it is for the purchase of imported oil. As I have advised my constituents who live in the western regions of the City of Montreal, most private car drivers are paying three or four times as much to drive to Montreal each day as compared with public transportation costs, even with the increased fares imposed by the

July 4, 1975
The Budget-Mr. Herbert
Canadian Pacific Railway. Greater use of public transportation might reduce losses and encourage improved service. If there is to be a subsidy paid by the taxpayer to the commuter, then it should be for public transportation.
I would like to refer briefly to housing. Despite cuts in almost every ministry, the Department of Urban Affairs has been allocated another $200 million to assist home building; that is another $200 million to be available for use before the end of this calendar year. These moneys will be added to the $1 billion that has already been committed this year to aid limited dividend projects, new home buyers, and non-profit housing.
Critics of the housing policies of the government should not forget the provincial responsibilities in the field of construction. It is the provincial governments that permit questionable hiring practices and limited apprenticeship training programs that lead to greater inefficiencies and higher costs. It is the provincial governments which, through their control over land usage, can stop speculation, retard or encourage development, and assist municipalities through servicing, if they so wish. As of this moment, whilst the federal government has already committed 80 per cent of this year's funds for housing, the provinces have only taken up a little over 50 per cent of the moneys available to them.
In my own constituency of Vaudreuil much local publicity was given to a provincial grant of three quarters of a million dollars for sanitary trunk collector sewers. In the municipality of Notre-Dame de l'lle Perrot, no publicity was given to the assistance of the federal ministry of urban affairs which provided loans totalling $1.2 million, with a forgiveness feature of $300,000. I mention this specific case, not because it is important to stress the relative participation of our three levels of government, but to illustrate that three levels of government are directly involved and are therefore jointly responsible for the number of housing starts in the country.
Whilst there has been a slowdown in housing construction on the west island of Montreal, one cannot fail to see the large numbers of houses being built today. The credit for this rests almost entirely with the imaginative mayors and councillors of these towns and municipalities who, by proper land planning and zoning, have provided servicing to lots that can be purchased at reasonable price levels. The tremendous growth in recent years in the town of Kirkland is an excellent illustration. The newly-announced multimillion dollar residential development on tie Bizard is another.
I am going to make a brief reference to the new local initiatives program referred to in the budget. I have suggested on previous occasions that these moneys were being used as a sort of stop-gap approach. At the same time I have been promoting a renewal of the very successful capital winter works program. We are now to see the best features of these two programs combined. There will also be an additional benefit for municipalities in my constituency. Under the capital winter works program the province of Quebec had established a $50,000 minimum or floor. Many of the municipalities that could not participate because of the minimum program size will be able to apply for assistance under the new local initiatives program.

Before I conclude, Madam Speaker, I want to make a couple of suggestions, neither of which will result in the spending of more money. On the contrary, the implementation of my recommendations could result in an increase in efficiency in the two areas to which I will refer, and probably in a cost saving without in any way diminishing federal government programs.
My first suggestion deals with the present approach to our export trade. A constituent of mine in Pierrefonds wrote me recently to express his disappointment with remarks I made in this House on May 28. The House was in committee of the whole studying the estimates of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Members were restricted to a time limit of 15 minutes, and I chose to use my time allocation to start to discuss the complex involvement in our export effort of nine ministries and over 20 Crown or proprietary corporations. It is my intention to expand on this subject at some future date.
Today I will limit myself to stating that I am now fully convinced that interdepartmental rivalries result in duplicated effort or, what is undoubtedly worse, an inadequate effort in selling this country's products, services, and potential in foreign markets. Maybe the answer is a minister responsible for all exports. At least the present complex machinery should be reviewed and restructured.
My second suggestion is directed to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) and deals with the many research programs of the several departments that have a research involvement.
My studies in the last couple of years have clearly identified the inefficiencies that result from the divided responsibilities so carefully guarded by the different departments. Does it make any sense, for example, that medical research should be divided between the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the National Research Council, scores of private groups, and even our genial Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)?
I understand that one of the main objectives of the Ministry of Science and Technology is the supervision and co-ordination of our research effort. I suggest that this objective be given high priority treatment.
I started my remarks by recording my congratulations to the Minister of Finance. When times are difficult, a budget has to be unpopular. I am proud to be associated with a government party that has had the guts to introduce this budget at this time and I support, without reservation, the approach of the budget and all the measures included therein.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, since this is the last day of the budget debate it is certainly obvious that the ground has been well covered by my colleagues on both sides of the House, and particularly by those on this side in respect of its many weaknesses. I have really tried to find something good to say about the budget but this has been a very difficult task, a very difficult one.
I guess we can give the minister some credit for one or two items in the budget. The first is in respect of the job
July 4, 1975

creation programs on which the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) elaborated for so long today. These programs will be of real advantage to my province of Newfoundland, particularly as the minister indicated that $450 million will be spent on job creating plans and that the new local initiatives program, involving $285 million, will be carried out on a 2-year basis with, perhaps even more important, great emphasis being placed on municipal works and projects. This is something I have been advocating ever since LIP started, but I qualify this by stating it should really be carried out on a 5-year basis.
Even though there has been much criticism from all parts of the country of LIP since it started, it has been of immense value to the rural parts and smaller communities in my province. I can safely say that many of the citizens in my district can be proud of the projects they have completed, as would the minister himself if he would look at some of them.
Many projects have been carried out, such as the construction of wharfs and breakwaters for fishermen, community, recreational and medical centres for local citizens, as well as water and sewage systems, all of which I suggest were constructed at far less cost than had they been carried out under government contract. At the same time they created employment for the local people and fulfilled the objectives of the citizens using their own initiative.
However, too many projects have been left uncompleted, causing needless waste of funds. This is because of a lack of control, a lack of guidance and counselling, a lack of co-ordination between various departments of government, and a lack of ensuring that particular community councils or any form of local government were included in the planning stages, thus leaving them in utter frustration and discouragement.
For example, literally dozens of fish stores, which are so vital to the execution of the fishing industry in many smaller communities in Newfoundland and the Atlantic region, were constructed and are now left unused because the people were not aware of the quality control measures introduced by the Department of the Environment. As a result, provincial governments are now burdened with the responsibility of finding the necessary dollars to cover the cost of installing the required measures.
Water and sewage systems were installed in various sections of a community in conflict with municipal and provincial planning where vast sums of funding were allocated for engineering planning of an over-all water and sewer system for the community, thus causing a waste of funds and a duplication of effort. It would have been so simple to co-ordinate the planning for the project with the involvement of the three levels of government concerned.
I have found over the years in which LIP has existed that the greatest benefit can be derived from grassroot level community planning, still achieving the local initiative aspect and still allowing private groups or organizations to participate, but not independently. They could participate by inserting another step before the project is vetted by the federal-provincial team that vets projects, allowing the local government to assess the project from a planning point of view on behalf of the community as a whole.
The Budget-Mr. Marshall
By planning the program on a 5-year basis the local governments could submit their priority needs from an economic, resource, and public service aspect. Over that period of time most local needs could be fulfilled and, more important, could be carried out again by the local citizens, thus instilling in them the pride and fulfillment of building up their own communities and creating employment. Certainly this should be true of the thousands of rural communities and smaller municipalities across Canada.
I should also like to suggest to the government that the Local Initiatives Program is being carried out by the wrong department. It is true that the Department of Manpower and Immigration should be involved, but only from an employment and training aspect. I suggest that the program should be carried out by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which is now so heavily involved in infrastructure funding and in rural and economic development. That department can do almost anything for the various regions under the general development agreement concept.
The Department of Regional Economic Expansion could do a better job of co-ordinating the needs of Canada. There was no need either to break down the job-creating funding as announced by the minister. In this regard I would pose several questions. Why separate the $70 million to training in industry and in educational institutions when the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has so many programs already in existence, so that no one knows how to get through the jungle to decide which is for what? Why separate another $25 million to finance labour-intensive federal projects where unemployment is most severe when the funding is still allocated on the basis of population and the size of the region?
While I am on this particular matter, let me ask why projects are carried out in the winter months? I suggest this is because someone within the department has said that unemployment is higher in the winter time. They do not have the commonsense to realize that the unemployment rate in some regions is just as high in the summer. If the projects could be carried out during the summer months in those areas, more value could be derived for the dollars spent, for obvious reasons.
Why separate another $10 million to be devoted to existing job placement and mobility programs? People would not have to move under mobility programs if jobs could be provided in their own localities. The manpower training programs represent a series of duplications and triplications, as well as confusion. I say with no embarrassment that the adult occupational program has done much for the uneducated and the unemployable, but what better basis of training and placement could be provided than by on-the-job training through the many and varied projects that could be carried out in the interest and for the development of rural communities across Canada? With a little ingenuity this would provide training methods in a practical way while the work was being carried out under the guidance of trained instructors.
So I say we have enough programs under the Department of Manpower. We have enough programs such as the

The Budget-Mr. Marshall
outreach programs, the job creation programs, the community employment strategies, the stepping stone programs which I noted the other day as a new one, and many others.
The 600,000 or 700,000 unemployed in Canada want jobs. Contrary to the thinking that too many of our citizens are taking advantage of our welfare and unemployment programs, these same people are begging for jobs which cannot be provided. I say with all sincerity that if the minister wants to practice restraint and at the same time create jobs, and still at the same time provide for the needs of our nation, then he should review the situation along the lines that I have suggested, and I am sure Canada would be better off.
I would like to say further that I am not at all sure the minister is moving in the right direction in restraining $100 million in capital expenditures of public works, environment, and other departments, because this is in direct conflict with what he is trying to accomplish in his job creation program; but in the interest of agreeing that we cannot have it both ways I am willing to go along with it with the exception of public works and environment because this relates to me that the fishermen in the Atlantic region will lose out on the provision of small craft harbours and other fishing facilities, which will deter and postpone again their ability to compete, taking advantage of the fishing industry, which would provide a boost to our economy and increase their ability to earn a livelihood.
I have to agree with the minister when he is restraining the spending required to create the Federal Business Development Bank, which to my mind is a waste of money. The present Industrial Development Bank is merely being given a new name, when all that was necessary was to expand the terms of reference of the Industrial Development Bank to provide counselling and management services, which is really all that is being done. Further, it is almost an exact duplication of the various federal provincial development loan corporations whose terms of reference are almost the same. Certainly, however, he could have gone a little further in reviewing the large bureaucracy which has been built up in the various loan programs, which does nothing more than confuse Canadians who are trying to take advantage of the programs.
I hesitate to mention the number of these programs, but my last count showed somewhere in the vicinity of 28 loan programs all directed on a hodge-podge basis to Canadians whether they be farmers, fishermen, or small businessmen. Those could all be amalgamated into one obvious responsibility under the minister's department.
I am pleased to note that the minister is placing a general limitation on consultant's fees and travel by public servants. It would be interesting to see the bill for the many thousands of public servants who are flitting around the country accomplishing nothing in most cases other than to show a presence, which is the job of the member of parliament. I am disappointed to note that no reference was made to evaluating the cost of Information Canada, which is in direct conflict with the 28 or so information services branches of each individual department of government, and is a waste of many millions of dollars. Certainly the minister would be better served if he were to examine, through the Auditor-General's

department, an evaluation of the objectives being served through the wanton, ridiculous spending that is going on because of lack of ability by ministers to control and examine the spending by their departments through no fault of their own, but because they are victims of the system which has long been out of control.
Much mention has been made of the increased price for gasoline and fuel oil. Here again I fail to see how the minister will effect a return of $350 million from this source, when rather what really he is doing is hurting the majority of taxpayers who will be affected, and chasing away tourist dollars, not to mention the nightmare he will face in trying to administer the program he suggests to relieve certain individuals or groups for whom he proposes to soften the blow. What he is really doing is hurting again the very Canadian who keeps being hit with inflationary costs, the middle and low income earners because they happen to be unfortunate enough to be in the majority. There is not much need to repeat the logical reasons given by the many who refer to this measure as a saving; but again it will be interesting to have revealed next year, when we examine the net figures, if the figure of $350 million will be realized.
The minister revealed also with pride the allocation of the funding of $200 million to bring housing starts to the rate needed in the long run to meet the housing needs of Canadians. While I admit certainly this will help to an extent in the Assisted Home Ownership Program, the limited dividend rental projects, and other non-profit programs, he is missing a great opportunity to assist hundreds of thousands of Canadians and relieve or postpone the need for housing starts which his colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs and Housing (Mr. Danson), cannot meet, about which he is rightfully disturbed, and at the same time help the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in his direction of effort to conserve fuel both on a federal and provincial basis.
I refer again, as I have many times before, to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance program, the Neighbourhood Improvement Program and the Rural and Native Housing Program, and even home improvement loans, which are designed to upgrade the many hundreds of thousands of homes across Canada that are substandard in quality and which are deteriorating to a substandard state because owners cannot afford to maintain them to decent standards due to inflationary costs of building materials and which, for the purposes of this particular exercise, could be upgraded to a longer life and thus save millions of gallons of fuel oil when brought up to a reasonable standard.
Under the RRAP program the minister could do so much by directing the funding toward allowing Canadians under the forgiveness factors of the program, to insulate properly their homes, as well as provide adequate heating and electrical needs. Unfortunately I did not have the time to research the number of homes in Canada that fall within this category, but I am sure that the minister could obtain the figures from Statistics Canada, from CMHC, or from the Canada Council on Social Development which has pointed out to the government the need to upgrade the homes of those citizens earning up to $11,000, under this program, which would effect a saving of literally millions
July 4, 1975

of gallons of heating oil to the particular consumers falling within this category.
I ask the minister to consider using the example of my province where many thousands of homes fall within this category, and ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) how much is expended in the cost-sharing program with the province of Newfoundland because of the need each year from November to May to provide additional funds to welfare recipients so that they can pay the increased cost of fuel oil, during the harsh winters, to heat their substandard housing.
I ask him to consult with his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, to direct the team of bureaucrats whom he has hired to teach Canadians ways to conserve fuel, if they have even thought of this aspect of conservation. I ask the minister to find out how many thousands of citizens there are who cannot afford to provide insulation for their homes because of cost-not only those who are on welfare but also those who fall in the low and fixed income brackets. I would ask him to find out how many thousands of homes falling within this category could be brought up to reasonable standards to relieve the pressure on the Minister of Housing in his dilemma, until he can catch up to the need for housing for all Canadians.
I ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) why such a program was not extended to the many thousands of veterans on War Veterans Allowances, the disability pensioners, or the widows of those veterans who are left alone on fixed pensions, to provide them with the same relief available under the National Housing Act but not directed on the priority basis which he should follow?
The minister gave a little nibble when he announced that the 5 per cent sales tax on insulation materials would be removed, affecting all purchases of insulating materials such as double pane glass, storm windows, and storm doors. But he has completely missed the point because he could have been of so much greater assistance by expanding the residential rehabilitation assistance program to allow those in greatest need to be able to afford the insulation material, the double pane glass windows, the storm windows and the storm doors. I can only ask him to take a closer look at this program which would be of so much benefit to so many Canadians who are hard pressed by inflation. All that is being saved as a result of the removal of the tax would be about $25 or $30.
In the interest of saving time I should like to speak on the decrease in the medical care cost-sharing program with the provinces, but I am sure the minister will face much battling on this score because of the pressure that will be brought on the provinces.
There are also many other items that one can discuss in the budget, but I only hope the minister will see the light and soften the blow to those Canadians who are suffering under inflation before the legislation which will put these measures into effect comes before the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am proud to serve on the same side of the House with Canada's present Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, oh!
The Budget-Mrs. Holt

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
During his three years in this portfolio he took important steps to spare Canadians the impact of the international economic crisis that has so shaken our long time friends and neighbours, the United States, Britain, the still free nations of Europe, and our major trading partner, Japan. Compared to the hyper-inflation which they have been experiencing, we seem untouched by the vice of inflation and recession. Comparatively speaking, Canada has weathered these troubled times so far with less pain and discomfort, thanks to our Minister of Finance.
Economic, political, and philosophical problems which were impossible to foresee have been forced on all of us by unsophisticated nations which suddenly achieved wealth of a magnitude and type never before seen in this world. At the same time moving in on the surviving free democratic societies like predators are two large communist powers.
This is strong language to describe the international vultures, picking off the bones of toppling freedom around the world. In essence, the primitive political masses are tools for the totalitarian power brokers. In these times, times of fear and uncertainty, the government has succeeded in cushioning the impact and assuring Canadians minimum suffering in health, welfare, housing, and energy in times of crisis. Remember that it is a time of economic crisis.
The Minister of Finance's newest budget is realistic action that surely must bring a sense of relief to Canadians who want strength and leadership. Canadians are not stupid people; they know that economically we are balanced on a precipice which needs shoring up. The protracted uncertainty and fear must certainly be eased in this nation, knowing we have leadership and strength to bring us out of this.
Surely most Canadians knew this good, excessively rich life could not last. It was over abundance and over indulgence. The dollar bill alone too long has been the measure of the quality of life. It is and has been the true worship of Mammon, without respect for human values. We were of course content to live above our means, living the hedonist life of joy now. Do not worry about tomorrow, was the prevalent motto. The poor have been surrounded by what in other times would be considered luxuries of those born with the silver spoon; the middle class in what was the bounty of the excessively rich; the rich becoming millionaires, and the millionaires becoming multimillionaires. Our society is said to have more millionaires today than ever before.
It is necessary for me to trace current history in order to make several points that are of importance at this time. First, my reason for favouring and even extending cutbacks in government spending-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There were cut-backs but you never noticed because you were not listening.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We are contemplating your next negative words.
7310

July 4, 1975
The Budget-Mrs. Holt
Second, I wish to correct misleading statements made in the House which suggest that inflation was unilaterally created.
Perhaps the most sobering event in the life of all people of the industrial society is the shift of power that has come with the contrived 1974 international energy crisis. Small nations, dominated and controlled by a few people, established cartels to control the life blood of industry and economy as well as the world's money. At least 40 countries, lacking self-sufficiency through resources, were left destitute. A handful of resource-rich nations controlled the world destiny by selfish use of the most decisive instrument of contemporary power, namely, oil.
They established a boycott, using oil to manipulate the world powers against the small state of Israel. Large industrial nations, including the United States, Japan, and the European states, were among their victims. Oil prices quadrupled, and the Group of 13, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, familiarly called OPEC, virtually took control of the money and the economy of the world in months, if not weeks.
In the post budgetary reaction, or second guessing, to increased prices of domestic gas and oil, those who shed printer's ink or politically advantageous tears were either immature, incapable of adult analysis of the world situation, or too blind or unwilling to see what was looming on the economic horizon of this nation.
Surely any thinking person knows that in this global village, caught by global inflation, we cannot resolve the problem started by excessive prices of the irreplaceable commodity, oil. No nation alone, unilaterally, can beat the tidal wave of inflation set off primarily by petro-dollars and the insatiable monopoly greed. The oil producing nations received $1 a barrel at the start of this decade, $3.44 by the end of 1973, $10 a year later, and now $12.
There are intelligent people on the other side of the House. I do not like to go to extremes and say they are overly endowed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thanks!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unfortunately they are so wedded to their own negativism, their political posturing, their simplistic formula solutions to complex world problems, that they cannot see, or do not care to see, or choose not to be impeded by the fact that Canada is caught in the complex dichotomy of inflation with recession. Canada's finance minister, recognizing the risks-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Caused by the Liberals.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is simple economy, and if you cannot see it, God help you.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: God will have to, the Liberals cannot.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Canada's finance minister, recognizing the risks facing Canada originally, established a single fixed national price for crude oil at $6.50. But there was obviously no way to ensure exploration or to slow Canada's continued reckless use, even waste, of oil that was cheap,

half the international price at that time. It is still comparatively cheap at $8 compared to the $12 of OPEC.
It is essential that we take preventive action, such as the Minister of Finance has undertaken to preserve our future. It must be done now while the people of Canada are still able to buy, while this government can still afford to support public needs and indeed public demands for support and services such as housing, health and, in effect, a guaranteed income for all. We must move; we cannot wait. We owe it to the next generation.
There are those trying to tell the public that the housing aspect of the budget is tokenism. That is an absolutely irresponsible and hurtful statement to the people of Canada. Certainly social need always has and always will move faster than the solutions. But $200 million in additional allocation for housing in the next 5 months along with what is already happening is significant and important. These things are being done before this country gets to the state of hyper-inflation and deep recession being experienced in the United States, Britain, and the other countries.
Let us hope this budget will prevent hyper-inflation devastating Canada as it has elsewhere. We can still assure the elderly and the working poor of what is in effect a guaranteed income and give an assurance that housing, medical and pharmaceutical needs are met. This government started all this virtually guaranteed income.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Surely you don't believe that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What did you do? You had your chance. Where are those who were supposed to start it?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
